The officers involved, who had received a report of a runaway child less than an hour earlier, will be investigated by the Bureau of Criminal Apprehension to determine whether criminal charges are warranted. Bells' mother later told news sources she believed Bells ran from foster care and evaded police while trying to return home to Cass Lake. Investigators later found that Bells stole a neighbor's car after entering their unlocked, unoccupied home to take the keys. Although the vehicle's registered address was over 10 miles away, the operator left it at the house neighboring the foster home that night. While the vehicle was registered to an older male, it was primarily driven by their teenage stepson, which is why high school football equipment was found on scene. Police reports say a deputy's body camera captured the vehicle in the driveway at 1.14 a.m. while searching for Bells following the runaway report. This was just 15 minutes before the pursuit began. Bell's older sister told news outlets she likely wasn't familiar with the difference between running lights and headlights. She stated, I can't even imagine what she was feeling at the time for her to feel the need to steal a car. She shouldn't have been able to run away. She's obviously very traumatized. The reasons for her removal from her parents' care have not been made public. Though some reports say she was previously found with peers driving a stolen vehicle, suggesting a troubled history. Regarding officer conduct, the Atasca County Pursuit Policy acknowledges the dangers pursuits posed to the public, officers, and suspects. It states, deputies must balance their duty to apprehend with public safety, using common sense and sound judgment, noting that immediate apprehension is generally less important than public safety. The policy also states that deputies who choose not to initiate a pursuit, even when circumstances permit one, will not face discipline, acknowledging that pursuits can be unpredictable. Factors deputies should consider when deciding whether to end a pursuit include, and are not limited to the seriousness of the crime, whether the suspect's identity is known, and if they pose a risk without apprehension, the time of the day, traffic in road conditions, vehicle speeds, and the age of those involved, if known. The policy discourages extended pursuits for nonviolent misdemeanors. Lastly, the policy state supervisors share responsibility for pursuit decisions and must assess whether a pursuit is justified. It also requires supervisory approval before using intervention tactics such as pit maneuvers or stop sticks. While supervisory approval is generally viewed as a safe approach, some argue requiring approval will delay split-second decisions often required in pursuits and unintentionally prolong the danger. Regarding this situation, the pursuing deputy stated they were aware that there was a runaway report of a 13-year-old girl. However, they also stated they did not believe the vehicle was related as the registration check came up with an older male and suspected a drunk driver. This is despite a Minnesota state trooper stating over radio that he would not pursue due to a belief that the driver could be bells. Possible juvenile driver, I'm not going to be involved here. He further states in his report that state policy doesn't permit the pursuit of a 13-year-old driver. However, that occurred on the state patrol channel which deputies were not monitoring. The patched to a statewide common channel heard by all officers in the state only occurred after this radio traffic. All of these factors were reportedly weighed by the BCA, who determined the officers would not be referred for prosecution for the incident or Bell's death. The report directly states that the deputy's actions were reasonable and that Bell's death was the result of her own decisions. Moreover, she was not wearing a seatbelt in video analysis indicates that Bells didn't apply the brakes prior to the crash. Bell's family posted a GoFundMe in support of funeral funds. The GoFundMe is still active at the time of posting this video and can be found in the description below.
